title: Chapter 25 — Of Discipline In Democratic Armies
paragraphs: It is a very common opinion, especially in aristocratic countries, that the great social equality prevailing in democracies eventually makes the private soldier independent of the officer, and so destroys the bond of discipline. This is a mistake, for there are two kinds of discipline, and it is important not to confuse them. When the officer is noble and the soldier a serf — one rich, the other poor, the former educated and strong, the latter ignorant and weak — the strictest bond of obedience can easily be established between the two men. The soldier is broken in to military discipline, so to speak, before he ever enters the army. Or rather, military discipline is nothing but an intensification of social servitude. In aristocratic armies the soldier soon becomes insensible to everything but the orders of his superior officers. He acts without reflection, triumphs without enthusiasm, and dies without complaint. In this state he is no longer a man, but he is still a most formidable animal trained for war.

A democratic people must give up hope of ever obtaining from soldiers that blind, minute, submissive, and unvarying obedience which an aristocratic people can impose on them without difficulty. The state of society does not prepare them for it, and the nation might be in danger of losing its natural advantages if it tried artificially to acquire advantages of this particular kind. Among democratic communities, military discipline should not try to annihilate the free spring of the faculties. All that discipline can do is direct it. The obedience thus instilled is less exact, but it is more eager and more intelligent. It has its root in the will of the one who obeys. It rests not only on his instinct but on his reason. And as a result it will often spontaneously become stricter as danger requires. The discipline of an aristocratic army is apt to be relaxed in war, because that discipline is founded on habits, and war disturbs those habits. The discipline of a democratic army, on the contrary, is strengthened in sight of the enemy, because every soldier then clearly sees that he must be silent and obedient in order to conquer.

The nations that have performed the greatest military achievements knew no other discipline than the one I am speaking of. Among the ancients, only freemen and citizens were admitted into the armies. They differed little from one another and were accustomed to treating each other as equals. In this respect the armies of antiquity may be called democratic, even though they came out of the bosom of aristocracy. The result was that in those armies a sort of fraternal familiarity prevailed between the officers and the men. Plutarch's lives of great commanders furnish convincing examples of this: the soldiers were in the constant habit of addressing their general freely, and the general listened to and answered whatever the soldiers had to say. They were kept in order by language and by example, far more than by constraint or punishment. The general was as much their companion as their chief. I do not know whether the soldiers of Greece and Rome ever carried the minutiae of military discipline to the same degree of perfection as the Russians have done. But this did not prevent Alexander from conquering Asia — or Rome, the world.
